case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 suit seeking only prospective declaratory and injunctive relief that would necessarily imply the invalidity of the plaintiff’s still-outstanding conviction under the challenged ordinance.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (with the background relationship to federal habeas statutes, particularly 28 U.S.C. § 2254/§ 2255 custody-based limits, and constitutional claims such as the First and Fourteenth Amendments as the basis for alleging the municipal ordinance is unconstitutional).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Olivier argues Heck’s “favorable termination” requirement should not bar (or should be substantially limited as to) forward-looking relief under §1983. He contends that when a plaintiff seeks only prospective declaratory/injunctive relief against future enforcement—rather than damages or direct invalidation of a past judgment—the suit is not the functional equivalent of habeas and should be permitted even if success would logically cast doubt on the earlier conviction. He also advances (at least as an alternative theme reflected in argument) that Heck’s rationale is to prevent an end-run around habeas, so it should not apply (or applies with less force) where the plaintiff lacked meaningful access to habeas because he was never “in custody” (or was not in a form of custody that made habeas realistically available).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City argues Heck applies whenever success in the §1983 action would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an existing criminal judgment—regardless of whether the plaintiff seeks damages or prospective relief. Because a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would call the prior conviction into question, Olivier must first obtain a favorable termination (e.g., reversal, expungement, habeas relief) before proceeding in §1983. Respondents further emphasize federalism/comity/finality concerns and maintain this case has additional procedural and merits obstacles (e.g., forfeiture/waiver, estoppel, res judicata) that would likely defeat relief even if Heck were narrowed.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Spencer-based fairness concern highlights a potential remedial gap, but as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, our precedents draw the line at whether success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, not at the plaintiff’s choice of prospective remedies. Wilkinson v. Dotson reinforces that §1983 remains available only where success would at most yield a new proceeding or otherwise not logically negate the conviction; here petitioner concedes a facial declaration/injunction against the very ordinance of conviction would undercut the still-valid judgment. Because Spencer’s separate opinions never commanded a majority, I would not narrow Heck via an equitable exception in this posture, and I would decide only that Heck bars this specific claim while the conviction stands, leaving any “no-habeas-access” question for a case that cleanly presents it. That narrow approach best preserves precedent, finality, and institutional legitimacy without foreclosing §1983 challenges that do not collide with an extant criminal judgment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the Spencer concurrence’s fairness concern that applying Heck when habeas is impractical could leave some plaintiffs without a federal forum, but that equitable rationale cannot override Heck’s operative, categorical “necessarily imply the invalidity” test. As Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan emphasize, Wilkinson reinforces that the bar applies “no matter the relief sought” when success would logically negate an outstanding conviction, and petitioner’s requested facial declaration/injunction against the very ordinance of conviction does exactly that. Under a textualist/originalist approach, §1983 supplies no basis for engrafting a “no-habeas-access” exception, and Spencer’s separate writings—lacking a majority—cannot narrow Heck’s holding. I therefore agree with the Chief Justice’s narrow approach: apply Heck here without opining on a hypothetical case where habeas is truly unavailable and the requested relief would not necessarily undermine an extant judgment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-based reliance on Justice Souter’s Spencer concurrence is the best argument for petitioner, but it cannot displace Heck’s operative rule: a §1983 action is not cognizable if success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding conviction absent favorable termination. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, petitioner concedes that a facial declaration/injunction against the very ordinance of conviction would logically negate the still-valid judgment, making this suit a collateral attack regardless of its prospective label. Wilkinson v. Dotson, as Justice Gorsuch notes, preserves §1983 only where success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction (e.g., at most a new proceeding), and that limiting principle is what maintains finality and comity in the Preiser/Heck framework. Whatever the equitable appeal of a no-habeas-access exception, Spencer’s separate opinions did not command a majority, and creating that carveout here would effectively rewrite Heck in a way our precedents do not support.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the hardest point: that a facial declaration/injunction against the ordinance of conviction would, in logic, negate the legal basis of an outstanding judgment and so falls within Heck’s “necessarily imply” language. But I do not read Heck as a free-floating logical-implication test divorced from its functional purpose (policing §1983 end-runs around habeas where habeas is the realistically available route to contest custody), and Wilkinson v. Dotson supports that pragmatic focus by preserving §1983 for forward-looking relief that does not operate as the functional equivalent of speedier release. Even taking Justice Gorsuch’s “no matter the relief sought” phrase seriously, that must be confined to claims whose civil success would operate as a direct collateral attack on custody, not suits aimed at preventing future enforcement where habeas is unavailable or illusory and the plaintiff otherwise lacks a meaningful federal forum. Spencer’s fairness concerns (though in separate writings) remain central to my methodology: I am unwilling to extend Heck in a way that effectively immunizes unconstitutional laws from prospective challenge by vulnerable speakers solely because they live under an outstanding conviction they cannot realistically clear through habeas.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the Spencer-based equity concern that, where habeas is unavailable in practice, a strict favorable-termination prerequisite can leave constitutional claims without a federal forum. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Heck’s operative rule is the “necessarily imply” test, and petitioner concedes that a facial declaration/injunction against the ordinance would negate the legal basis for his still-outstanding conviction—making this a collateral attack regardless of its prospective label. Wilkinson v. Dotson, which Justice Kavanaugh and I have relied on, preserves §1983 only when success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction (e.g., at most a new proceeding), not when the civil judgment would logically unravel the extant criminal judgment. The Spencer concurrence’s remedial-gap worry may justify revisiting Heck in a case cleanly presenting no meaningful habeas avenue, but it does not warrant carving an exception here in a posture that squarely triggers Heck’s implication bar.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the Spencer-based fairness concern that applying Heck where habeas is practically unavailable can leave constitutional claims without a federal forum, especially for forward-looking relief. But Heck’s operative rule is not a purpose-driven balancing test; it asks whether success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction, and (as the Chief Justice notes) petitioner concedes his requested facial declaration and injunction would negate the legal basis of his still-valid judgment. Wilkinson, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, preserves §1983 for prospective relief only when success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction (e.g., at most a new proceeding), which is not this case. However sympathetic the remedial-gap concern, Spencer’s separate writings did not command a majority and §1983’s text supplies no “no-habeas-access” exception we may legitimately engraft consistent with separation-of-powers and finality principles.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness argument, drawing on the Spencer v. Kemna concurrence, is the strongest counterpoint, but it cannot displace Heck’s holding that §1983 is not cognizable when success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction absent favorable termination. As the Chief Justice stresses, petitioner concedes that a facial declaration/injunction against the very ordinance of conviction would logically negate the legal basis of his still-valid judgment, so this case falls squarely within Heck’s “necessarily imply” bar. Wilkinson v. Dotson, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, preserves §1983 only where success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction (e.g., at most a new proceeding), and the “prospective” label cannot avoid that logical implication. Creating a no-habeas-access exception here would require a significant doctrinal revision based on nonmajority Spencer writings and would raise serious administrability and end-run concerns contrary to Heck/Preiser finality and comity interests.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the Spencer/Souter fairness concern: if habeas is unavailable, applying Heck risks leaving some constitutional claims without a federal forum. But Heck’s operative, administrable rule—bar §1983 claims whose success would “necessarily imply” invalidity of an outstanding conviction absent favorable termination—does not turn on the plaintiff’s access to habeas, and this case fits squarely within that categorical test because, as the Chief Justice notes, petitioner concedes his requested facial declaration would negate the legal basis for his still-valid conviction. Wilkinson v. Dotson, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress, preserves §1983 only when success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction (e.g., it yields at most a new procedure); it therefore does not support a prospective-relief carveout where invalidity is the logical consequence. Whatever the equities, creating a “no-habeas-access” exception here would require narrowing Heck based on nonmajority Spencer writings and would invite line-drawing problems and end-runs around finality/comity that Heck and Preiser sought to protect.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the Spencer-based remedial-gap concern—procedural fairness when habeas is unavailable or illusory—but on this record that equity does not defeat Heck’s operative “necessarily imply” test. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, petitioner concedes that a facial declaration that the very ordinance of conviction is unconstitutional would logically negate the legal basis for an outstanding judgment, making the §1983 action function as a collateral attack regardless of its prospective label. Wilkinson v. Dotson, cited by multiple colleagues, reinforces that §1983 remains available for forward-looking relief only when success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction or sentence; that distinction is not satisfied here. Consistent with my pragmatic approach, I would leave open whether a narrow no-habeas-access exception is ever warranted, but this case is not the vehicle because the requested relief directly collides with the still-valid conviction.

John Roberts.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 action when “a judgment in favor of the plaintiff would necessarily imply the invalidity of his conviction or sentence,” and petitioner concedes that a facial declaration invalidating the ordinance would logically undermine his still-outstanding conviction. Wilkinson v. Dotson preserves §1983 for prospective relief only where success would not necessarily spell invalidity; it does not authorize end-runs around Heck when the requested declaratory/injunctive relief would negate the legal basis of the conviction. Given the institutional and federalism interests in finality and comity, the narrow, precedent-following resolution is to apply Heck’s favorable-termination rule here rather than carve a new prospective-relief exception untethered to the “necessarily imply” standard. Any adjustment for plaintiffs allegedly lacking realistic habeas access is better left for a case that cleanly presents that issue without requiring us to rewrite Heck’s operative rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1983 creates a cause of action for deprivations of federal rights, but it does not authorize a collateral attack on a still-valid criminal judgment; under Heck v. Humphrey, a §1983 claim is not cognizable where success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction absent favorable termination. A facial declaratory judgment and injunction against enforcement of the very ordinance of conviction would necessarily imply that conviction’s invalidity, and Wilkinson v. Dotson does not alter that result because it permits §1983 only where success would not necessarily invalidate the judgment or shorten custody. Allowing this suit would undermine finality and invite end-runs around the limits Congress placed on postconviction review in 28 U.S.C. §§2254/2255, contrary to Heck’s rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey holds that a §1983 action is not cognizable when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding criminal judgment absent a favorable termination, and that rule turns on the necessary logical implication, not on whether the plaintiff labels the requested remedy “prospective.” A facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would undercut the legal basis for Olivier’s still-valid conviction and thus squarely triggers Heck’s bar, reflecting the same finality and comity concerns that animate the habeas/§1983 boundary (28 U.S.C. §2254) identified in Heck and Preiser. Wilkinson v. Dotson does not compel a different result because it permitted §1983 only where success would not necessarily spell invalidity of the conviction or sentence; here, petitioner’s requested relief would do precisely that. Extending an exception for prospective relief would invite end-runs around criminal judgments and burden law-enforcement and municipal enforcement with collateral federal litigation before the conviction is set aside.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination rule is best understood as a pragmatic limit designed to prevent §1983 from becoming an end-run around habeas when habeas is actually available, not as a blanket jurisdictional bar on all forward-looking relief under 42 U.S.C. §1983. Where a plaintiff seeks only prospective declaratory and injunctive relief against future enforcement, the suit is not the functional equivalent of habeas relief under 28 U.S.C. §2254/§2255, and Wilkinson v. Dotson supports permitting §1983 actions that do not seek immediate or speedier release even if success undermines aspects of a prior judgment’s logic. Moreover, as Justice Souter explained in Spencer v. Kemna (concurring), it is unfair and impractical to impose a favorable-termination prerequisite that is impossible to satisfy for plaintiffs lacking meaningful habeas access, leaving constitutional claims without any realistic federal forum. Construing Heck to bar this prospective challenge would unduly insulate unconstitutional ordinances from review and disproportionately burden vulnerable speakers by forcing them to live under ongoing threat of enforcement without an effective remedy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey holds that a §1983 action is not cognizable when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction unless that conviction has been favorably terminated, and that logic turns on avoiding an end-run around the habeas framework (28 U.S.C. §§2254/2255) and preserving finality. Here, a facial declaration and injunction against enforcement of the ordinance—given petitioner’s still-outstanding conviction under that ordinance—would logically entail that the conviction rests on an unconstitutional law and is therefore invalid, triggering Heck’s bar regardless of the remedy requested. Wilkinson v. Dotson permits prospective relief only where success would not necessarily spell invalidity of the conviction or sentence (e.g., it would at most lead to a new proceeding), and Edwards v. Balisok likewise recognizes prospective relief is ordinarily available only when it does not necessarily imply invalidity. A categorical “prospective-relief exception” would be hard to square with Heck’s text and would be administratively unworkable, inviting artful pleading to circumvent the favorable-termination requirement embedded in the §1983/habeas boundary.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey holds a §1983 action is not cognizable when “a judgment in favor of the plaintiff would necessarily imply the invalidity of his conviction or sentence” unless the conviction has been favorably terminated, 512 U.S. at 486–87, and that logic is not limited to damages. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms the dividing line turns on whether success would necessarily demonstrate the invalidity of the outstanding judgment, and that such claims may be barred “no matter the relief sought,” 544 U.S. at 81–82. Because a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would necessarily call into question Olivier’s still-outstanding conviction under that ordinance, §1983 cannot be used to obtain that result without first satisfying Heck’s favorable-termination requirement (with habeas-like finality and separation-of-powers concerns counseling against expanding §1983 beyond the limits this Court has recognized). Arguments about limited access to habeas may raise hard equities, but they do not justify rewriting Heck’s necessarily-imply rule as applied to an extant criminal judgment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination rule bars §1983 actions when success “would necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding criminal judgment, and petitioner concedes that a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would logically cast his still-valid conviction into doubt. Wilkinson v. Dotson and Edwards v. Balisok preserve room for forward-looking relief when it does not necessarily imply invalidity of the conviction or sentence, but here the requested declaratory/injunctive relief would do exactly that, triggering Heck’s comity and finality concerns at the intersection of §1983 and the habeas framework (28 U.S.C. §2254/§2255). Limiting Heck based on the plaintiff’s asserted lack of meaningful habeas access would require a significant narrowing of settled doctrine and invite practical line-drawing problems and collateral federal attacks on state judgments inconsistent with precedent and institutional stability. The proper course is to require favorable termination first and leave prospective challenges that do not undermine an existing judgment to proceed under §1983 as Wilkinson contemplates.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey held that a §1983 action is not cognizable when “a judgment in favor of the plaintiff would necessarily imply the invalidity of his conviction or sentence” unless the conviction has been favorably terminated, and that rule is best read to turn on the logical effect of success, not the label of the remedy sought. A facial declaratory judgment that the ordinance is unconstitutional would necessarily call into question Olivier’s still-outstanding conviction under that ordinance, so the suit functions as an impermissible collateral attack absent favorable termination. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms the dividing line: §1983 is available only where success would not “necessarily spell speedier release” or otherwise necessarily invalidate the conviction or sentence; here, by concession, success would imply invalidity. Whatever the equitable appeal of a “no-habeas-access” exception, §1983’s text contains no such carveout, and creating one would be a methodological departure from Heck’s precedent-based harmonization of §1983 with the habeas statutes (28 U.S.C. §§2254/2255).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 action when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction unless the plaintiff first obtains a favorable termination, and a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would logically call Olivier’s still-existing conviction into question. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that the §1983/habeas boundary turns on whether the civil judgment would necessarily undermine the conviction or sentence, not simply on whether the plaintiff styles the remedy as prospective, and Edwards v. Balisok applies the same logic to claims that would invalidate the basis for punishment. While Spencer v. Kemna’s separate opinions suggest narrowing Heck when habeas is unavailable due to lack of “custody,” that view did not command a majority and does not override Heck’s operative rule where (as the record indicates) probation/suspended sentence may constitute custody for habeas purposes under 28 U.S.C. §2254/§2255. Given those precedents and the finality/comity concerns Heck sought to protect, the suit is barred absent favorable termination even though Olivier seeks only declaratory and injunctive relief under 42 U.S.C. §1983.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 action seeking purely prospective declaratory and injunctive relief that would necessarily imply the invalidity of the plaintiff’s existing criminal conviction (and/or ongoing probationary consequences) under the challenged ordinance.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (and the Heck doctrine’s interaction with federal habeas statutes, principally 28 U.S.C. § 2254/§ 2255, plus underlying First Amendment/constitutional challenge to the municipal ordinance).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Olivier argues that Heck’s “favorable-termination” bar should not apply (or should be narrowed) when a §1983 plaintiff seeks only forward-looking relief—i.e., a declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional (including facially) and an injunction against future enforcement—because such relief does not itself vacate or undo the prior conviction, and because applying Heck where the plaintiff lacks meaningful habeas access (e.g., not ‘in custody’ or never had custody in the relevant sense) would leave constitutional violations without a federal remedy. As a fallback, petitioner suggests a limiting rule under which Heck does not bar prospective relief unless the §1983 cause of action requires proving the prior conviction’s invalidity as an element.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City argues that Heck applies whenever success in the §1983 suit would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment, regardless of the form of relief requested; under Wilkinson and related cases, the same favorable-termination rule governs damages, declaratory relief, and injunctive relief when the civil judgment would call the conviction into question. Respondents emphasize petitioner’s concessions (and the United States’ concession in briefing) that a facial declaration of unconstitutionality would undermine the prior conviction, triggering Heck. They also press federalism/finality/comity interests and argue there are additional vehicle problems (forfeiture, estoppel/res judicata, and related litigation such as Siders) that could independently defeat relief even if petitioner prevails on the Heck question.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Spencer-based “Heck-without-habeas” concern is the most forceful objection, but Spencer’s discussion appears only in separate writings and supplies no controlling rule authorizing us to carve out an atextual exception to Heck’s favorable-termination requirement. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Wilkinson v. Dotson preserves §1983 only when success would not necessarily imply invalidity; here, the requested facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would logically negate the legal basis for an outstanding conviction carrying continuing probationary consequences, bringing the case within Heck and Edwards v. Balisok regardless of the prospective label. I am not persuaded we can reliably “tailor” relief, as Justice Sotomayor suggests, without effectively authorizing a collateral civil invalidation of the judgment in substance if not in form. A narrow affirmance applying Heck on these facts preserves precedent and institutional legitimacy while leaving any true no-habeas-access exception for a cleaner vehicle.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “Heck-without-habeas” concern is the strongest equitable argument, but under a textualist approach it cannot justify crafting an atextual exception to §1983 or narrowing Heck absent support in the statute’s original public meaning. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the controlling inquiry under Heck/Wilkinson is whether success would “necessarily imply” invalidity; a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would, in substance, negate the legal basis for an outstanding conviction with continuing probationary consequences, making the suit a collateral attack. Edwards confirms plaintiffs cannot evade that rule by relabeling the requested remedy as prospective or declaratory. Spencer’s remedial-gap discussion, as several colleagues note, appears only in separate writings and supplies no governing rule for us to adopt in this posture; any gap is for Congress to address.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the Spencer “Heck-without-habeas” remedial-gap concern, but equitable unease cannot justify reworking Heck’s favorable-termination rule where the §1983 claim’s success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction with continuing probationary consequences. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Wilkinson v. Dotson preserves §1983 only when success would not necessarily call the conviction into question; a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional does negate the legal basis for the still-operative judgment, and Edwards v. Balisok confirms that relabeling the remedy as prospective does not avoid Heck’s bar. Sotomayor’s proposed tailoring of forward-looking relief lacks a principled stopping point and would invite end-runs around habeas/direct review, undermining finality and comity in precisely the way Heck sought to prevent. Spencer’s separate writings are noncontrolling and, on these facts, do not undermine the practical “necessarily imply” test we are bound to apply.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s workability concern seriously: Wilkinson and Edwards make clear we look to whether success would “necessarily imply” invalidity, not to the label on the relief. But I do not accept the premise—pressed by Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett—that a prospective injunction/declaration against future enforcement of the ordinance, carefully framed, must logically negate the still-outstanding conviction; a court can enjoin ongoing unconstitutional applications without purporting to vacate, expunge, or otherwise adjudge invalid the prior judgment and its existing legal consequences. Where habeas is not meaningfully available, Spencer’s remedial-gap problem (though not controlling) is a powerful reason, under a pragmatic and access-to-justice lens, to resist extending Heck to foreclose the only federal forum for an ongoing restraint. Courts can police end-runs by scrutinizing the remedial scope and denying relief that in substance alters the conviction, but they should not categorically bar all forward-looking relief whenever a conviction exists.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Spencer “Heck-without-habeas” point is the hardest equity problem here, but it does not squarely answer Heck’s operative inquiry: whether success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment. On this record, the requested facial declaration and forward-looking injunction would, in substance, negate the legal basis for a still-operative conviction with ongoing probationary consequences—exactly the situation the Chief Justice (invoking Wilkinson) and Justice Barrett emphasize is barred regardless of the damages/prospective label. I agree with Justice Roberts that Spencer’s remedial-gap discussion is noncontrolling and cannot support crafting an administrability-heavy carveout that would invite artful pleading to evade Heck’s channeling rule. I would affirm narrowly on the ground that where the §1983 relief necessarily undermines an extant conviction, favorable termination is required, leaving any true no-habeas-access exception for a cleaner vehicle.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the Spencer “Heck-without-habeas” remedial-gap concern, and I agree it has equitable pull; but as the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize, our precedents make the dispositive question whether success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment. A facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would negate the legal basis for petitioner’s still-operative conviction and probationary consequences, bringing the case within Heck and Edwards regardless of how the relief is styled, and Wilkinson preserves §1983 only when that necessary-implication link is absent. Spencer’s separate writings do not supply a governing exception we may graft onto §1983, and under separation-of-powers principles any adjustment to the §1983/habeas boundary is for Congress or a different case that squarely presents true habeas unavailability without directly undermining an extant judgment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the Spencer “Heck-without-habeas” remedial-gap concern and her contention that a forward-looking injunction/declaration can be cabined to future enforcement. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Wilkinson v. Dotson and Edwards v. Balisok make the controlling question whether success would “necessarily imply” invalidity, and a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would, in substance, negate the legal basis for an outstanding conviction with ongoing probationary consequences. Spencer’s separate writings underscore an equitable problem, yet they are not a holding narrowing Heck, and adopting a prospective-relief carveout here would invite relabeling end-runs that erode finality and comity—concerns that, institutionally, we should not discount absent clearer guidance from precedent or Congress. I would therefore affirm on the narrow ground that Heck applies on these facts, while leaving any true no-habeas-access exception for a cleaner vehicle.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the Spencer “Heck-without-habeas” remedial gap and her claim that prospective relief can be tailored to avoid negating the conviction, but that tailoring premise fails under Heck’s controlling “necessarily imply” inquiry as applied to these facts. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would, in substance, erase the legal basis for an outstanding conviction with ongoing probationary consequences, bringing the case within Heck and Edwards regardless of the forward-looking label. Spencer’s separate opinions do not supply a holding we can graft onto §1983, and under a textualist/originalist methodology we should not create an atextual exception that reallocates to §1983 what Congress and our precedents have channeled through habeas/direct review. I would therefore affirm on narrow grounds, leaving any true no-habeas-access exception for a cleaner vehicle.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—the Spencer “Heck-without-habeas” remedial-gap concern—has real equitable pull, especially where ongoing restraints persist but habeas relief may be illusory. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Wilkinson and Edwards tie the §1983/habeas line to whether success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment, and a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would, in practical effect, negate the legal basis for a still-operative conviction with probationary consequences. Spencer’s gap discussion is not a holding that authorizes us to craft an administrable prospective-relief carveout here, and adopting one in this posture risks destabilizing Heck by inviting relabeling of collateral attacks. On a progressive pragmatic view attentive to systemic consequences and workable rules, the narrower course is to apply Heck on these facts and leave any no-habeas-access adjustment for a case that squarely presents it without directly undermining an extant judgment.

John Roberts.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 action when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding criminal judgment, and that concern is not avoided simply by styling the request as declaratory or injunctive relief rather than damages. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson and Edwards v. Balisok, the operative inquiry remains whether the requested relief would, in substance, call the existing conviction or sentence into question, thereby intruding on habeas’ channeling function under 28 U.S.C. §§ 2254/2255 and undermining finality and comity. Here, petitioner’s requested facial declaration of unconstitutionality would necessarily imply the invalidity of his still-operative conviction and attendant probationary consequences, so a narrow disposition is to apply Heck’s favorable-termination requirement and leave any broader “no-habeas-access” exceptions for another case with a cleaner vehicle. That approach adheres to precedent and avoids a disruptive reworking of the §1983/habeas boundary with significant federalism implications.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1983’s text contains no exception allowing a civil action to proceed when success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment, and Heck v. Humphrey properly adopted a favorable-termination requirement in that circumstance to preserve the finality of criminal convictions and respect the habeas-specific remedial scheme in 28 U.S.C. §§ 2254/2255. Under Heck’s “necessarily imply” test, a prospective declaratory judgment that the ordinance is facially unconstitutional would, as a matter of logic, call into question the legal basis for petitioner’s existing conviction and any continuing probationary consequences, so the suit is barred absent favorable termination. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that the governing inquiry is not the label of relief (damages vs. declaratory/injunctive) but whether the §1983 judgment would necessarily demonstrate the invalidity of the conviction; Edwards v. Balisok likewise applied Heck where success would imply invalidity. Whatever the equitable appeal of providing a federal forum, courts may not revise Heck’s rule based on perceived remedial gaps when the conviction remains outstanding and unvacated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey holds that a §1983 action is barred when success “would necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding criminal judgment, and that principle is best read to turn on the practical effect of the civil judgment, not on whether the plaintiff styles the relief as declaratory or injunctive. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson and Edwards v. Balisok, §1983 remains available for prospective relief only when success would not necessarily call into question the validity of the conviction or sentence; here, petitioner’s requested facial declaration of unconstitutionality would logically undermine the existing conviction and ongoing probationary consequences. Allowing such a suit would function as an end-run around the habeas/§1983 boundary at the core of Heck and would erode finality and comity by inviting collateral attacks in federal court outside the mechanisms Congress provided in 28 U.S.C. §§2254/2255. Whatever hard cases may exist where habeas is unavailable, this case—given the necessary implication conceded—falls within Heck’s bar.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination requirement was fashioned to prevent an end run around habeas (28 U.S.C. § 2254/§ 2255) and to avoid using § 1983 as a de facto vehicle to overturn a conviction, but that rationale weakens sharply when the plaintiff seeks only prospective declaratory/injunctive relief and lacks meaningful habeas access (the “Heck-without-habeas” problem flagged by multiple Justices in Spencer v. Kemna). Extending Heck to bar all forward-looking relief would leave many people—especially those with only probationary or expired sentences—without any federal forum to stop ongoing constitutional injuries from an allegedly invalid ordinance, undermining § 1983’s remedial purpose and access to justice. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that § 1983 remains available where success does not necessarily entail immediate or speedier release, and here the requested remedy can be cabined to future enforcement rather than vacatur of the past judgment. At minimum, Heck should not bar prospective relief unless the § 1983 claim requires proving the conviction’s invalidity as an element or the injunction would operate to terminate the conviction’s continuing legal consequences directly.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 action when success would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment, and petitioner’s requested facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would, as a matter of logic, call his existing conviction (and continuing probationary consequences) into question. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that the relevant line is not the label of relief (damages vs. declaratory/injunctive), but whether the §1983 judgment would necessarily undermine the conviction or sentence; here it would, unlike Wilkinson’s challenges to procedures that could lead to a different outcome only in the future. Reading Heck this way best harmonizes §1983 with the habeas statutes (28 U.S.C. §§2254/2255) and serves workability and finality by avoiding parallel federal civil judgments that effectively negate still-valid state convictions. Any narrowing based on “elements” of the §1983 claim would be hard to administer and would invite end-runs around Heck’s coherent favorable-termination requirement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1983’s broad text does not itself contain a favorable-termination requirement, but Heck v. Humphrey supplies a limiting rule where a civil judgment would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding criminal judgment, preserving the distinct role Congress assigned habeas (28 U.S.C. §§ 2254/2255) for attacking convictions. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, the critical line is whether success “will not necessarily imply” invalidity; here, petitioner’s requested declaratory/injunctive relief—especially a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional—would logically call the existing conviction and its ongoing probationary consequences into question, triggering Heck’s bar. Accepting petitioner’s categorical prospective-relief carveout would require rewriting Heck’s necessarily-imply test and would invite an end-run around finality and separation-of-powers principles by allowing §1983 to perform habeas’s work. Whatever the equities when habeas is unavailable, that is a policy question for Congress, and this Court’s precedents (including Edwards v. Balisok’s application of Heck beyond damages) point to applying the bar when the civil theory negates the criminal judgment’s validity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 suit when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding criminal judgment unless the conviction has been favorably terminated, and that rule is best read to apply irrespective of whether the plaintiff seeks damages or declaratory/injunctive relief. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms §1983 remains available for prospective relief only when success would not necessarily spell invalidity; here, a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would directly call the existing conviction (and any ongoing probationary consequences) into question. Extending an exception for prospective relief would cut against Heck’s reconciliation of §1983 with habeas (28 U.S.C. §§ 2254/2255) and would undermine finality and comity by permitting collateral attacks on criminal judgments via civil litigation. Whatever the equities for plaintiffs with limited habeas access, that policy argument is for Congress or a narrower case; under precedent and a workability/legitimacy approach, the Fifth Circuit’s application of Heck should be affirmed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey holds that a §1983 action is not cognizable when “a judgment in favor of the plaintiff would necessarily imply the invalidity of his conviction or sentence” unless the conviction has been favorably terminated, and that rule turns on necessary implication, not on the plaintiff’s choice of damages versus equitable relief. Wilkinson v. Dotson preserves §1983 for prospective challenges that would not necessarily spell invalidity, but it does not authorize a §1983 suit whose success would itself call an outstanding criminal judgment into question; Edwards v. Balisok likewise reflects that prospective relief is ordinarily permissible only when it does not necessarily imply invalidity. Here, a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional (and an injunction against its enforcement as applied to plaintiff) would necessarily undermine the validity of an extant conviction and ongoing probationary consequences under that ordinance, so the claim falls within Heck’s bar absent favorable termination through habeas or analogous relief under 28 U.S.C. §2254/§2255 principles.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey holds that a §1983 action is barred whenever success “would necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding criminal judgment, and that logic is not avoided by styling the request as declaratory or injunctive relief if the requested judgment would functionally call the conviction into question. Wilkinson v. Dotson and Edwards v. Balisok confirm that the relevant inquiry is the necessary implication for the criminal judgment, not the remedial label, and a facial declaration that the ordinance is unconstitutional would logically undermine the validity of Olivier’s existing conviction and continuing probationary consequences. While Spencer v. Kemna highlighted the ‘Heck-without-habeas’ remedial gap in concurrences/dissents when habeas is unavailable to non-custodial plaintiffs, that view has not been adopted as a controlling limitation on Heck’s bar, and expanding §1983 here would risk undermining finality/comity protections that Heck was designed to preserve. On these facts, the proper route to invalidate an outstanding judgment remains favorable termination via direct review or habeas (where available), rather than a §1983 suit whose success would negate the conviction’s legal foundation.
